How to use this sheet: you do not need any background to read it. Start with Key Terms. Each concept then goes: plain English → analogy → 3 core points → for every formula: what it says, when to use it, what each letter means, an everyday example, a step-by-step MCAT example and the trap → where to practice. Read top to bottom once, then use the formulas as a reference.

Key terms (read first)

TermPlain meaning
Δ (delta) and Σ (sigma)Δ means "change in" (final − initial). Σ means "add them all up".
Molecule / reactionA molecule is a group of bonded atoms. A reaction rearranges molecules: reactants (starting materials) turn into products.
CoefficientThe number in front of a substance in a balanced equation (the 2 in 2H₂O): how many of it react or form.
Mole (mol) / concentration [X], MA mole is a counting unit, 6.022 × 10²³ particles. [X] = concentration of X; M = moles per liter.
Energy, joule (J), kJEnergy is the capacity to do work or heat something. A joule is a small unit (lifting an apple 1 m takes about 1 J); 1 kJ = 1,000 J.
Temperature, kelvin (K)Temperature measures how fast particles jiggle. Kelvin = °C + 273.15; 0 K is absolute zero. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.
Pressure (P), atmForce pushing on an area. 1 atm = normal air pressure at sea level (= 760 torr ≈ 1.013 bar).
Volume (V), LSpace taken up, in liters.
PhaseSolid, liquid or gas.
Intermolecular attractionsWeak "stickiness" between separate molecules; breaking them is what melting and boiling require.
System / surroundingsThe part you are studying (the reaction) / everything else. Open systems exchange matter and energy, closed exchange only energy, isolated exchange neither.
State functionA quantity that depends only on the current state, not on how you got there (U, H, S, G, P, V, T). Heat (q) and work (w) are path functions.
Internal energy (U)Total energy stored in the system's particles.
Heat (q)Energy transferred because of a temperature difference; q > 0 means heat flows into the system.
Work (w)Energy transferred by a force acting through a distance; for gases, pressure–volume work. Here w > 0 means work done on the system.
Isothermal / adiabaticIsothermal = at constant temperature. Adiabatic = no heat enters or leaves (q = 0).
Enthalpy (H)Heat content at constant pressure; ΔH = q_p. ΔH < 0 is exothermic (releases heat), ΔH > 0 endothermic (absorbs heat).
Standard state (°)1 atm (1 bar) for gases, 1 M for solutes, pure solids/liquids, usually 25 °C. Biochemical standard (°′) also sets pH 7.
Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f)ΔH for making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states; zero for elements in standard state (O₂(g), C(graphite)).
Bond enthalpyEnergy needed to break one mole of a given bond in the gas phase.
Entropy (S)How spread out energy and particles are (the number of ways, or microstates, to arrange them); "disorder."
Reversible processAn idealized, infinitely slow change that can be undone without leaving any trace in the surroundings.
Gibbs free energy (G)Energy available to do useful work at constant T and P; ΔG < 0 means spontaneous.
SpontaneousHappens on its own without continuous outside input; says nothing about speed.
ATPThe cell's energy currency; breaking off a phosphate (hydrolysis) releases about 30 kJ/mol of free energy.
EquilibriumThe state where forward and reverse reactions run at the same speed, so amounts stop changing (dynamic: both still happen).
Equilibrium constant (K) and reaction quotient (Q)Products over reactants (raised to their coefficients) at equilibrium (K) or right now (Q). Pure solids and liquids are left out.
Partial pressureThe share of total gas pressure due to one gas.
Gas constant (R)A fixed number linking energy, temperature and amount: 8.314 J/(mol·K), or 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) for pressure problems.
log, ln, elog = base-10 logarithm (log 1,000 = 3). ln = natural log, base e ≈ 2.718; ln x ≈ 2.303 log x. e^x is the opposite of ln.
Specific heat (c) / heat capacity (C)Heat to raise 1 g by 1 °C / heat to raise a whole object by 1 °C.
CalorimeterAn insulated container used to measure heat from a reaction by the temperature change of water or the device.
Vapor pressureHow strongly molecules escape from a liquid into gas. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure.
Fusion / vaporization / sublimation / depositionMelting / boiling (liquid → gas) / solid → gas directly / gas → solid directly.
Phase diagram, triple point, critical pointA map of which phase is stable at each pressure and temperature. Triple point: all three phases coexist. Critical point: above it, liquid and gas become one "supercritical fluid".
RateHow fast a concentration changes, in M/s.
Rate lawEquation linking reaction rate to reactant concentrations: rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ; x and y are found by experiment.
Rate constant (k)Proportionality constant in the rate law; changes with temperature and catalysts, not with concentration.
OrderThe exponent on a concentration in the rate law; overall order is their sum.
Collision theoryMolecules react only when they collide with enough energy (at least Ea) and in the right orientation.
Elementary step / mechanismA single molecular event / the sequence of steps that makes up the overall reaction. Molecularity = how many molecules collide in one step.
Rate-determining stepThe slowest step in a mechanism; it limits the overall rate.
IntermediateMade in one step and used up in a later step; sits in a valley on an energy diagram.
Transition stateThe highest-energy, fleeting arrangement at the top of an energy hill; cannot be isolated.
Activation energy (Ea)Energy barrier from reactants up to the transition state.
Catalyst / enzymeA catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering Ea; it is regenerated at the end and does not change ΔG or K. Enzymes are protein catalysts.
Half-life (t½)Time for half of a reactant to be used up.
Hemoglobin (Hb)The oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells.

A) CORE CONCEPTS

Concept 1: Systems, state functions and the first law

In plain English: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only moved. A system's stored energy goes up when heat flows in or when something does work on it (squeezes it), and goes down when it gives off heat or does work (pushes outward).

Analogy: Internal energy is a bank balance. Heat and work are deposits and withdrawals. The balance (a state function) only depends on what is in the account now, not on whether you got there with one big deposit or many small ones.

Official definition: The first law states that energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals heat added to the system plus work done on the system, ΔU = q + w, with expansion work w = −PΔV at constant external pressure.

Core idea (3 points):

  • State vs. path: state functions (U, H, S, G, P, V, T) are path-independent; q and w are not. Closed systems exchange energy but not matter; isolated systems exchange neither.
  • Sign convention (chemistry): q > 0 heat absorbed; w > 0 work done on the gas (compression); a gas that expands does work on the surroundings (w < 0). At constant pressure with only PV work, q_p = ΔH; at constant volume, w = 0 and q_v = ΔU.
  • Special cases: ideal gas, isothermal: ΔU = 0, so q = −w. Adiabatic (q = 0) expansion: the gas does work using its own internal energy, so it cools. Third law: a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0.
ΔU = q + ww = −P<sub>ext</sub>ΔV

In plain words: the change in stored energy equals heat put in plus work done on the system; when a gas expands against an outside pressure, the work is negative (the gas spent energy pushing).

When to use it: questions giving heat and work values and asking for ΔU, or a gas expanding/compressed against a constant outside pressure and asking for work. Cue words: "absorbs heat", "does work on the surroundings", "expands against 1 atm". When it does not apply: w = −PΔV needs a constant external pressure; it is 0 if the volume does not change (rigid container). Watch for physics books that use ΔU = Q − W with W = work done by the gas.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔUChange in internal energyJNet change in the bank balance
qHeat added to the systemJ+ in, − out
wWork done on the systemJ+ when compressed, − when it expands
P_extExternal (opposing) pressureatm (or Pa)What the gas pushes against
ΔVVolume change (final − initial)L (or m³)1 L·atm = 101.3 J

Everyday example: Your bank account. Your paycheck deposits $500 (heat in, q = +500) and you pay $200 rent (work done by you, w = −200). Balance change = 500 + (−200) = +$300. It does not matter whether the rent left before or after the paycheck came in.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings: ΔU = (+500) + (−200) = +300 J.
  2. A gas expands from 2.0 L to 5.0 L against 1.0 atm: ΔV = +3.0 L, so w = −(1.0)(3.0) = −3.0 L·atm.
  3. Convert: −3.0 × 101.3 J/(L·atm) = −304 J.

MCAT trap: Mixing sign conventions. Some physics books write ΔU = Q − W (W = work done by the gas). In chemistry's ΔU = q + w, work done by an expanding gas is negative.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (not a state function), (first law sign convention), (compression and heat release), (closed system), (third law), (isothermal expansion), (adiabatic expansion cools), (w = −PΔV).

Concept 2: Enthalpy, Hess's law and enthalpies of formation

In plain English: Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat a reaction releases or absorbs. Because it depends only on start and finish, you can calculate it three ways: from tabulated "formation" values, by adding up steps (Hess's law), or roughly from bond strengths.

Analogy: Hess's law is a hiking altitude change. Whether you take the switchback trail or the direct cliff path, going from the parking lot to the summit changes your altitude by the same amount, because altitude (enthalpy) is a state function.

Official definition: Enthalpy change is the heat exchanged at constant pressure; because H is a state function, ΔH for an overall reaction equals the sum of ΔH for any series of steps (Hess's law), and can be computed from standard enthalpies of formation or estimated from bond enthalpies.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Manipulating ΔH: reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH; multiplying a reaction by n multiplies ΔH by n. ΔH scales with amount: if 2.0 mol releases 1,600 kJ, 0.25 mol releases 200 kJ.
  • Formation values: ΔH°f of an element in its standard state is 0 (O₂(g), N₂(g), C(graphite)). ΔH°f of NaCl(s) is the ΔH for Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s) (exactly 1 mol of product, elements in standard states).
  • Bond enthalpies (gas phase averages) give only estimates; ΔH°f values are more accurate. Breaking bonds is always endothermic; reactions that form stronger bonds than they break are exothermic. N≡N has the largest N–N bond energy. A reaction that cools its vessel at constant P is endothermic.
ΔH°<sub>rxn</sub> = ΣnΔH°<sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣnΔH°<sub>f</sub>(reactants)

In plain words: the reaction's heat equals the total "formation energy" of everything you end with minus the total of everything you started with, each multiplied by how many moles appear in the equation.

When to use it: a question gives a table of ΔH°f values (kJ/mol) and asks for ΔH° of a reaction (combustion, metabolism of glucose, etc.). When it does not apply: use only standard-state ΔH°f values for the right phase (H₂O(l) ≠ H₂O(g)); with bond enthalpies the order is reversed (see below).

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔH°rxnStandard enthalpy change of the reactionkJ (per mole of reaction as written)Negative = exothermic
nStoichiometric coefficientmolMultiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient
ΔH°fStandard enthalpy of formationkJ/mol0 for elements in standard state

Everyday example: Elevations. You start at a spot 75 m below sea level (reactants, −75) and end at a mine shaft 966 m below sea level (products, −966). Your change = −966 − (−75) = −891 m: you went down 891 m. A negative ΔH means the products sit "lower" in energy, and the difference is released as heat.

MCAT worked example (step by step): CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), with ΔH°f CH₄ −75, CO₂ −394, H₂O(l) −286 kJ/mol.

  1. Products: −394 + 2(−286) = −966 kJ.
  2. Reactants: −75 + 2(0) = −75 kJ (O₂ is an element in its standard state).
  3. ΔH° = −966 − (−75) = −891 kJ.

MCAT trap: Forgetting the coefficients (using −286 once instead of twice) or giving O₂ a nonzero ΔH°f.

Hess's law: ΔH<sub>overall</sub> = ΔH<sub>1</sub> + ΔH<sub>2</sub> + ...

In plain words: if you can build the target reaction by adding up other reactions, its ΔH is the sum of their ΔH values (after flipping or scaling them as needed).

When to use it: questions giving two or three reactions with ΔH values and asking for ΔH of a different reaction that can be assembled from them, or asking what happens to ΔH when an equation is reversed or multiplied. When it does not apply: the steps must add up exactly to the target (cancel everything that is not in it); it works for any state function (ΔG, ΔS too) but never for path functions like q or w alone.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔH_overallEnthalpy of the target reactionkJThe summit altitude change
ΔH₁, ΔH₂Enthalpies of the steps, after flipping or scaling themkJFlip → change sign; × n → × n

Everyday example: A hike in two legs. Leg 1 goes down 394 m. Leg 2 is a trail you know goes down 283 m in the other direction, so walking it backward takes you up 283 m. Net change = −394 + 283 = −111 m, whatever route you took.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Target C(s) + ½O₂ → CO(g). Given (1) C + O₂ → CO₂, −394 kJ and (2) CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, −283 kJ.

  1. Keep reaction 1 as written: −394 kJ.
  2. Reverse reaction 2 (CO₂ → CO + ½O₂) and flip its sign: +283 kJ.
  3. Add: CO₂ and ½O₂ cancel, leaving the target. ΔH = −394 + 283 = −111 kJ. (Scaling check: if A → 2B is +80 kJ, then 4B → 2A = −2 × 80 = −160 kJ.)

MCAT trap: Reversing a step but forgetting to change its sign, or doubling the equation without doubling ΔH.

ΔH ≈ Σ(bond enthalpies broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies formed)

In plain words: the reaction's heat is about the energy needed to break the old bonds minus the energy released by making the new ones.

When to use it: a question gives bond energies (kJ/mol) instead of ΔH°f values, for gas-phase reactions. When it does not apply: it is an estimate (average bond values), less accurate than ΔH°f; it assumes everything is a gas; and the order is reactants − products, the opposite of the ΔH°f formula.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
Bonds brokenBonds in reactants that are brokenkJ/molEnergy cost (+)
Bonds formedBonds in productskJ/molEnergy released (−)

Everyday example: Renovating a kitchen. Tearing out the old cabinets costs $656 (breaking bonds). The new cabinets add $759 in value (forming bonds). Net = 656 − 759 = −$103: you come out $103 ahead, just as a reaction forming stronger bonds than it breaks releases heat.

MCAT worked example (step by step): CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl with C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 328, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol.

  1. Broken: one C–H + one Cl–Cl = 413 + 243 = 656 kJ.
  2. Formed: one C–Cl + one H–Cl = 328 + 431 = 759 kJ.
  3. ΔH ≈ 656 − 759 = −103 kJ. (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl with H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431: 679 − 862 = −183 kJ.)

MCAT trap: Using products − reactants with bond enthalpies. That order belongs to ΔH°f; for bond enthalpies it is broken (reactants) − formed (products).

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (why Hess's law works), (ΔH of CO formation), (reversing and scaling), (ΔH from ΔH°f), (ΔH°f of O₂), (formation reaction of NaCl), (scaling with moles), (H₂ + Cl₂ from bond energies), (chlorination of methane), (bond-energy estimates less accurate).

Concept 3: Entropy and the second law

In plain English: Energy and matter naturally spread out, because there are far more spread-out arrangements than tidy ones. Entropy measures that spreading. In anything that happens on its own, the total entropy of the universe goes up, even if one part gets more ordered.

Analogy: Entropy is like a teenager's bedroom: there are vastly more messy arrangements than tidy ones, so left alone, it drifts toward mess. Energy behaves the same way: it spreads out because there are more ways to be spread out.

Official definition: Entropy measures the dispersal of energy and matter (number of accessible microstates); the second law states that the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process (ΔS_univ > 0) and is unchanged in an idealized reversible process.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Signs of ΔS: ΔS > 0 for solid → liquid → gas; more moles of gas; dissolving a solid; mixing two gases; heating; expanding a gas at constant T. ΔS < 0 for freezing, condensing, fewer gas moles (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃), protein folding (of the chain itself).
  • Standard molar entropy rises with phase (gas ≫ liquid > solid), with molar mass and with molecular complexity. Temperature increases entropy because more energy levels become populated.
  • System vs. surroundings: a system's entropy can fall if the surroundings gain more (a hot block cooling heats the room; an exothermic reaction gives ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T > 0). Endothermic dissolving is spontaneous only if ΔS_system is large enough.
ΔS = q<sub>rev</sub> / TΔS<sub>surr</sub> = −ΔH<sub>sys</sub> / TΔS<sub>univ</sub> = ΔS<sub>sys</sub> + ΔS<sub>surr</sub>

In plain words: entropy change is heat moved (reversibly) divided by the temperature at which it moves; heat a reaction releases raises the surroundings' entropy; and the universe's total is the sum of both.

When to use it: ΔS of melting, boiling or freezing at the transition temperature (q_rev = ΔH_transition); ΔS of the surroundings for a reaction with known ΔH; "is this process spontaneous overall?" (ΔS_univ > 0). When it does not apply: ΔS = q/T needs reversible heat at a constant temperature in kelvin (a phase change at its normal transition point is the classic case); away from that, use tabulated entropies.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔSEntropy change of the systemJ/K (or J/(mol·K))+ = more spread out
q_revHeat transferred reversibly (e.g. at a phase transition)JHeat at the melting or boiling point
TAbsolute temperatureKSame heat matters more at low T
ΔS_surrEntropy change of the surroundingsJ/KExothermic reactions warm, and disorder, the surroundings
ΔS_univTotal entropy changeJ/K> 0 for any spontaneous process

Everyday example: A $100 gift means a lot to a student with $10 and little to a millionaire. Heat works the same way: 6,010 J added at a cold 273 K raises entropy by 6,010/273 ≈ 22 J/K, but the same 6,010 J added at a hot 600 K raises it by only ≈ 10 J/K.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. 1 mol of ice melts at 273.15 K with ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol = 6,010 J/mol.
  2. ΔS = 6,010/273.15 = +22.0 J/(mol·K).
  3. A reaction at 300 K with ΔH = −60 kJ: ΔS_surr = −(−60,000)/300 = +200 J/K.

MCAT trap: Using °C (0 °C) in ΔS = q/T, which divides by zero. Always convert to kelvin.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (second law), (reversible ΔS_univ), (negative ΔS), (most positive ΔS°), (highest standard entropy), (ΔS of melting ice), (mixing gases), (hot block cooling), (ΔS of surroundings), (endothermic dissolving).

Concept 4: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity

In plain English: Whether a reaction happens on its own depends on two things: whether it releases heat and whether it spreads things out. Gibbs free energy combines both into one number. Negative ΔG means "it will go"; it says nothing about how fast.

Analogy: ΔG is a reaction's "decision score." Enthalpy (ΔH) is the money you gain or lose; entropy (TΔS) is the freedom you gain, and temperature sets how much you value freedom. A negative score means the deal goes ahead on its own.

Official definition: At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a process is spontaneous when ΔG < 0, at equilibrium when ΔG = 0, and nonspontaneous when ΔG > 0. −ΔG equals the maximum non-expansion (useful) work available.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Sign table: (−ΔH, +ΔS) always spontaneous; (+, −) never; (−, −) spontaneous at low T; (+, +) spontaneous at high T. The crossover temperature is T = ΔH/ΔS. A plot of ΔG vs. T is a line with slope −ΔS and intercept ΔH.
  • Phase changes: at a phase transition (water boiling at 100 °C, 1 atm), ΔG = 0, so ΔS = ΔH/T. Ice melting above 0 °C is spontaneous though endothermic.
  • Speed and coupling: ΔG says nothing about rate (diamond → graphite is spontaneous but immeasurably slow). Unfavorable biochemical reactions are driven by coupling to ATP hydrolysis: ΔG values add.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

In plain words: the free-energy change equals the heat change minus temperature times the entropy change.

When to use it: "is it spontaneous at X K?", "above/below what temperature is it spontaneous?" (set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS), protein folding/unfolding, melting, dissolving, and coupled reactions. When it does not apply: it predicts direction, not speed; T must be in kelvin; and ΔH and ΔS must be in matching units (kJ and kJ/K). For the effect of concentrations, use ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔGGibbs free energy changekJ/molNegative = spontaneous
ΔHEnthalpy changekJ/molNegative helps
TAbsolute temperatureKScales how much entropy matters
ΔSEntropy changekJ/(mol·K) (convert from J!)Positive helps, more so at high T

Everyday example: Deciding on a gym membership. It costs $40 a month (ΔH = +40, a cost). It gives you 100 "freedom points" (ΔS = +100), and you value each point at $0.50 (T). Score = 40 − 0.50 × 100 = −10: a negative score, so you join. If you valued points at only $0.30, the score would be +10 and you would not. The break-even value is 40/100 = $0.40, just as the crossover temperature is ΔH/ΔS.

MCAT worked example (step by step): ΔH = −80 kJ/mol, ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K).

  1. Convert: ΔS = −0.200 kJ/(mol·K).
  2. At 500 K: ΔG = −80 − (500)(−0.200) = −80 + 100 = +20 kJ/mol (not spontaneous).
  3. Crossover: T = ΔH/ΔS = (−80,000)/(−200) = 400 K, so it is spontaneous only below 400 K (like a protein that unfolds above that temperature). Coupling: a +14 kJ/mol reaction + ATP hydrolysis (−30) = −16 kJ/mol, now spontaneous.

MCAT trap: Forgetting to convert ΔS from J to kJ. Using −200 instead of −0.200 gives ΔG = +99,920 kJ/mol, an absurd number.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (what ΔG < 0 means), (ΔH +, ΔS +), (never spontaneous), (ΔG at 500 K), (protein unfolding temperature), (ΔG = 0 at boiling point), (maximum useful work), (coupling with ATP), (ΔG vs. T plot), (diamond to graphite).

Concept 5: Free energy and equilibrium (ΔG°, ΔG, K and Q)

In plain English: Every reaction has a "natural balance point" (K) set by its standard free energy. Whether a real mixture moves forward or backward depends on how far it currently is from that balance point. At the balance point, nothing changes overall and ΔG is zero.

Analogy: ΔG° is the slope of a hill measured from a fixed starting line (standard conditions). ΔG is the slope where the ball actually sits right now (given Q). The ball rolls downhill until it reaches the bottom of the valley (equilibrium), where the slope is zero.

Official definition: The standard free-energy change sets the equilibrium constant, ΔG° = −RT ln K; the actual free-energy change depends on the current mixture, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K), and is zero at equilibrium.

Core idea (3 points):

  • ΔG° and K: K > 1 ↔ ΔG° < 0; K = 1 ↔ ΔG° = 0; K < 1 ↔ ΔG° > 0. At 298 K, 2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol, so each factor of 10 in K is 5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG°.
  • Q tells direction: Q < K → ΔG < 0 → reaction runs forward; Q > K → ΔG > 0 → runs in reverse; Q = K → ΔG = 0. A reaction with positive ΔG° still proceeds forward if Q is small enough (removing product makes ΔG more negative without changing ΔG°).
  • Temperature dependence (van 't Hoff): ln K vs. 1/T is linear with slope −ΔH°/R. A positive slope means ΔH° < 0 (exothermic: K falls as T rises).
ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K

In plain words: the standard free-energy change is minus a temperature-scaled logarithm of the equilibrium constant; every factor of 10 in K is worth about 5.7 kJ/mol at room temperature.

When to use it: converting between ΔG° and K ("K = 1.0 × 10⁻³; find ΔG°", "ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol; find K"), or judging whether products are favored at equilibrium. When it does not apply: it gives the standard value only; for the actual mixture use ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) with J (not kJ), and T in kelvin; the 5.7 kJ/mol shortcut is only for 298 K.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔG°Standard free-energy changeJ/mol (kJ/mol)Negative = products favored at equilibrium
RGas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K)J/(mol·K)Use J version here
TAbsolute temperatureK298 K gives 2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol
KEquilibrium constantunitless> 1 favors products

Everyday example: A sound meter. Every 10 decibels means 10 times more sound intensity, so 30 dB more is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times louder. Free energy works like decibels for K: every 5.7 kJ/mol is a factor of 10, so 17.1 kJ/mol = 3 × 5.7 = a factor of 1,000 in K.

MCAT worked example (step by step): K = 1.0 × 10⁻³ at 298 K.

  1. ΔG° = −(8.314)(298) ln(10⁻³) = −(2,478)(−6.91).
  2. ΔG° = +17,100 J/mol = +17.1 kJ/mol (shortcut: −5.7 × log K = −5.7 × (−3) = +17.1).
  3. Reverse direction: if ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol, log K = 11.4/5.7 = 2 → K = 100.

MCAT trap: Mixing kJ with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), giving answers off by 1,000; or saying "ΔG° = 0 at equilibrium." At equilibrium ΔG = 0; ΔG° is a fixed number that is generally not zero.

ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q

In plain words: the real-time free-energy change equals the standard value plus a correction for the current mix of products and reactants.

When to use it: questions giving ΔG° and current concentrations (or Q) and asking for ΔG or which way the reaction will go now; biochemistry questions where a reaction with positive ΔG°′ still runs in cells because products are removed. When it does not apply: Q is built like K (solids and pure liquids left out, coefficients as exponents); T in kelvin; units of RT must match ΔG° (RT = 2.48 kJ/mol at 298 K).

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔGFree-energy change for the current mixturekJ/molSign tells which way it will go now
ΔG°Standard free-energy changekJ/molFixed at a given T
QReaction quotient (current products/reactants)unitlessSmall Q pushes forward
RT2.48 kJ/mol at 298 KkJ/molConverts ln Q into energy

Everyday example: A shirt's list price is $10 (ΔG° = +10, not a great deal). The store is overstocked and offers a $17.10 rebate (the RT ln Q term when Q is small). Final price = 10 − 17.10 = −$7.10: they effectively pay you, so the "reaction" (buying) goes forward. The list price alone did not decide it.

MCAT worked example (step by step): ΔG° = +10 kJ/mol, Q = 1.0 × 10⁻³ at 298 K.

  1. RT ln Q = (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ/(mol·K))(298 K) ln(10⁻³) = (2.48)(−6.91) = −17.1 kJ/mol.
  2. ΔG = 10 − 17.1 = −7.1 kJ/mol: the reaction runs forward.
  3. Check at equilibrium: if ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol and Q = 10, ΔG = −5.7 + 5.7 = 0, so the mixture is already at equilibrium.

Concept 6: Calorimetry and heat capacity

In plain English: Different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up. Water needs a lot, metals very little. By measuring how much the temperature of water (or a sealed device) changes, we can work out how much heat a reaction released or absorbed.

Analogy: Specific heat is how "stubborn" a material is about changing temperature. Water is very stubborn (needs lots of heat per degree); metals are pushovers. In a calorimeter, the heat one thing loses is exactly the heat the other gains.

Official definition: Heat absorbed by a substance without a phase change is q = mcΔT; in an isolated calorimeter q_lost = −q_gained. A coffee-cup calorimeter (constant pressure) measures ΔH; a bomb calorimeter (constant volume) measures ΔU, using q = C_cal ΔT.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Water is stubborn: water's c = 4.18 J/(g·°C) (molar heat capacity 75 J/(mol·K)) is much larger than metals' (Al 0.90, Cu 0.39), which is why coastal temperatures swing less. With equal heat and mass, the lower-c metal (Cu) warms more.
  • Coffee cup: if the solution warms, the reaction released heat (ΔH < 0, q_rxn = −q_solution). Heat escaping to the room makes the measured |ΔH| too small.
  • Heat capacity C (J/°C) = m × c for a whole sample; a bomb calorimeter has its own calibrated C_cal.

In plain words: the heat needed equals the mass times how stubborn the material is (specific heat) times how many degrees the temperature changes.

Concept 7: Phase changes and phase diagrams

In plain English: When a substance melts or boils, the heat you add goes into pulling molecules apart instead of raising the temperature, so the temperature stays flat until the change is complete. A phase diagram is a map showing whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at any pressure and temperature.

Analogy: Heating ice is like filling stairs and landings. On the ramps (one phase) temperature climbs; on the landings (melting, boiling) all the heat goes into breaking intermolecular attractions, so the temperature stays flat until the phase change is finished.

Official definition: During a phase transition temperature stays constant while heat q = nΔH_transition (or mL) breaks or forms intermolecular attractions; a phase diagram maps the stable phase versus pressure and temperature, with phase boundaries, a triple point and a critical point.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Size of the heats: ΔH_vap ≫ ΔH_fus (vaporization must separate molecules completely). Steam burns are worse than water burns at 100 °C because condensing releases ΔH_vap (≈ 40.7 kJ/mol). Sweat cools by absorbing ΔH_vap. ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap. Heating-curve slope in one phase ∝ 1/(heat capacity).
  • Boiling point: vapor pressure = external pressure (normal bp at 1 atm). Lower pressure at altitude → lower bp. Raising T raises vapor pressure.
  • Phase diagram: triple point = all three phases coexist; above the critical point there is a supercritical fluid (no distinct liquid/gas). Water's solid–liquid line slopes left (ice is less dense than water), so pressure melts ice; most substances slope right. CO₂'s triple point (≈ 5.1 atm) is above 1 atm, so dry ice sublimes. Below the triple-point T, compressing a gas gives a solid directly (deposition).

Concept 8: Reaction rates and rate laws

In plain English: A rate law says how a reaction's speed depends on how much of each reactant is present. You cannot read it off the balanced equation; you find it by experiment, changing one amount at a time and watching what happens to the speed.

Analogy: A rate law is a recipe for how fast the kitchen works. Doubling an ingredient might double the speed (first order), quadruple it (second order), or do nothing (zero order) if that ingredient is not the bottleneck. You find out by tasting (experiment), not by reading the menu (the balanced equation).

Official definition: The rate law, rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, gives the dependence of rate on concentrations; the orders x and y are determined experimentally (method of initial rates) and equal the coefficients only for an elementary step; k depends on temperature and catalysts.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Rates from stoichiometry: for aA → bB, rate = −(1/a)Δ[A]/Δt = (1/b)Δ[B]/Δt. Initial rates are used so that reverse reactions and product buildup do not interfere.
  • Method of initial rates: change one concentration at a time; (rate ratio) = (concentration ratio)^order. 2× → 2× is first order; 2× → 4× second; 2× → no change zero.
  • Units and influences: units of k = M^(1−n)·s⁻¹ for overall order n: zero order M/s, first s⁻¹, second M⁻¹s⁻¹. Surface area (grinding a solid), temperature and catalysts increase rate; collision theory says collisions must have enough energy (≥ Ea) and the right orientation.

In plain words: the speed of a reaction equals a constant times each reactant's concentration raised to its own power (its order); add the powers to get the overall order.

When to use it: initial-rate tables ("find the rate law"), "what happens to the rate if [A] triples and [B] halves?", and finding k or its units. When it does not apply: the exponents come from data (or the slow elementary step), never from the balanced equation's coefficients; k changes with temperature, so compare runs at the same T.

Concept 9: Integrated rate laws and half-life

In plain English: Integrated rate laws tell you how much reactant is left after a given time. The half-life is how long it takes to lose half. For first-order processes, like most drug elimination and radioactive decay, the half-life never changes, so each half-life cuts the amount in half again.

Analogy: A first-order reaction is like a bag of popcorn where each kernel has the same chance to pop each second, no matter how many are left: the half-life never changes. A zero-order reaction is a vending machine giving out one can per minute regardless of stock. A second-order reaction slows down extra fast as partners become scarce.

Official definition: Integrating each rate law gives a straight-line plot: zero order [A] vs. t, first order ln[A] vs. t, second order 1/[A] vs. t; the half-life is constant for first order, shrinks as [A] falls for zero order, and grows as [A] falls for second order.

Core idea (3 points):

  • First order: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, slope −k; t½ = 0.693/k, independent of concentration (radioactive decay, most drug elimination). After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ remains.
  • Second order: 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt, slope +k; t½ = 1/(k[A]₀), so halving [A]₀ doubles t½.
  • Zero order: [A] = [A]₀ − kt (linear fall, e.g. absorbance dropping linearly); t½ = [A]₀/(2k), so t½ shortens as [A] falls (saturated enzymes, alcohol elimination).

Concept 10: Mechanisms and reaction coordinate diagrams

In plain English: Most reactions happen in several small steps. The slowest step controls the overall speed. An energy diagram draws the journey: hills are transition states (must be climbed), valleys between hills are intermediates (briefly exist), and the height of the first climb is the activation energy.

Analogy: A mechanism is an assembly line. The slowest station (rate-determining step) sets the factory's output. A reaction coordinate diagram is the hiking profile: transition states are mountain passes, intermediates are valleys between them.

Official definition: A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps whose sum is the overall reaction; the rate law is set by the slowest step (with fast pre-equilibria substituted to remove intermediates), and the reaction coordinate diagram shows energies of reactants, transition states, intermediates and products.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Elementary steps: the rate law follows the step's molecularity (2NO₂ → NO₃ + NO: rate = k[NO₂]²). Termolecular steps (A + B + C) are rare. Intermediates (made then consumed) never appear in the final rate law; catalysts are consumed then regenerated.
  • Examples: fast pre-equilibrium 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast), N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂ (slow) gives rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. Slow first step NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO gives rate = k[NO₂]² (CO is zero order).
  • Reading the diagram: Ea(forward) = E(TS) − E(reactants); ΔH = E(products) − E(reactants); n steps show n transition states and n − 1 intermediates. Endothermic: Ea(forward) > Ea(reverse). In plain words: the reaction's heat change equals the climb from the reactant side minus the climb from the product side.

Concept 11: Temperature, the Arrhenius equation and catalysis

In plain English: Reactions speed up when it gets warmer because more molecules have enough energy to get over the activation-energy hill. Catalysts (including enzymes) lower the hill, so the reaction goes faster in both directions, without changing where it ends up.

Analogy: Molecules trying to react are high-jumpers facing a bar (Ea). Raising the temperature gives more athletes a big enough jump (more molecules in the high-energy tail). A catalyst lowers the bar for jumps in both directions.

Official definition: The Arrhenius equation, k = A e^(−Ea/RT), links the rate constant to activation energy and temperature; raising T increases the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea, and catalysts provide a lower-Ea pathway, increasing forward and reverse rates equally without changing ΔG or K.

  • What changes k: only temperature and catalysts change k; concentration changes rate, not k. A (the pre-exponential factor) reflects collision frequency and orientation. A plot of ln k vs. 1/T is a line with slope −Ea/R; reactions with larger Ea are more temperature-sensitive.
  • Rule of thumb: rate roughly doubles per 10 °C near room temperature (so +30 °C ≈ 2³ = 8×).
  • Catalysts: lower Ea for both directions by the same amount, so K is unchanged (a 100-fold faster forward rate means a 100-fold faster reverse rate); added at equilibrium they cause no shift. Homogeneous (same phase) vs. heterogeneous (Pt surface in a catalytic converter). Enzymes stabilize the transition state. If rate = k[S][Cat], doubling catalyst doubles the rate.

Concept 12: The equilibrium constant and the reaction quotient

In plain English: At equilibrium a reaction is still running both ways, but the amounts stop changing. K is the fixed ratio of products to reactants at that point. Q is the same ratio for whatever mixture you have right now; comparing Q with K tells you which way the reaction will go.

Analogy: Equilibrium is a busy escalator pair: people ride up and down constantly, but the number of people on each floor stays the same. K tells you the final crowd ratio between floors; Q tells you the ratio right now, so you can predict which way the net flow will go.

Official definition: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant; K is the products-over-reactants expression (pure solids and liquids omitted); comparing Q with K predicts the direction of net reaction; for an elementary reversible step, K = k_forward/k_reverse.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Writing K: N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO → K = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]); CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → K = [CO₂] (or P_CO₂); water as solvent is omitted. K ≫ 1 (10¹⁵) = products essentially complete; K ≪ 1 = little product.
  • Manipulating K: reverse → 1/K; multiply equation by n → Kⁿ; add equations → multiply K values (K₁K₂ for A ⇌ C). Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
  • What changes it: only temperature changes K. Q = 0 at the start (no products). Q < K → forward; Q > K → reverse (ΔG > 0 for the forward direction).
K = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ)K = k<sub>forward</sub> / k<sub>reverse</sub> (elementary)

In plain words: K is the product concentrations multiplied together (each raised to its coefficient) divided by the same for reactants, measured at equilibrium; for a single step it also equals the forward rate constant divided by the reverse one.

When to use it: writing an equilibrium expression, calculating K from equilibrium concentrations, ICE-table problems (Initial, Change, Equilibrium), manipulating K for reversed/scaled/added equations, and relating K to rate constants. When it does not apply: leave out pure solids and liquids (and water as solvent); use equilibrium values only (current values give Q); K = kf/kr holds for an elementary step (or the overall product of steps), not for rate constants of an arbitrary rate law.

Concept 13: Le Châtelier's principle

In plain English: If you disturb a reaction at equilibrium (add or remove something, squeeze it, heat it), it shifts in the direction that partly undoes your disturbance. Only a temperature change actually changes K; the other changes just move the mixture until Q matches K again.

Analogy: An equilibrium is a stubborn seesaw that pushes back on whatever you do: add weight on one side and it tilts to use some of it up; squeeze the seesaw and it shifts toward the side that takes less room; warm it and it moves in the direction that soaks up heat.

Official definition: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure (volume) or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change; only a temperature change alters K, and catalysts or inert gases at constant volume cause no shift.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Concentration: add reactant or remove product → Q < K → forward shift (adding H₂ to the Haber equilibrium consumes some N₂; the new [H₂] is still higher than before). Removing Fe³⁺ from Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ shifts left (color fades).
  • Pressure via volume: compressing shifts toward fewer gas moles; no shift if gas moles are equal (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI). Adding argon at constant volume changes no partial pressures → no shift. Opening a soda lowers P(CO₂), so CO₂(aq) leaves solution.
  • Temperature: treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic). Heating favors the endothermic direction and changes K. Biology: at high altitude (low P_O₂), Hb + O₂ ⇌ HbO₂ shifts left; making more Hb pushes it back toward HbO₂.

Everyday example: A crowded bus. When more people get on at the front (adding reactant), riders shuffle toward the back (forward shift) until it feels evenly packed again. If the bus suddenly gets smaller (compression), people pair up and squeeze together (fewer "gas moles"). The bus never fully cancels the change; the front stays a bit more crowded than before.

Worked example (step by step): N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at equilibrium; the volume is halved.

  1. Both concentrations double, so Q = (2[NO₂])²/(2[N₂O₄]) = 4/2 × K = 2K.
  2. Since Q > K, the system shifts left (toward N₂O₄, fewer gas moles) until Q = K again.
  3. Contrast: 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ with Kc = 5.0 and [NO₂] = [N₂O₄] = 0.50 M gives Q = 0.50/0.50² = 2.0 < 5.0, so it shifts forward.

MCAT trap: Saying compression changes K. Compression changes Q (and the position), not K; only temperature changes K.

Concept 14: Kinetic vs. thermodynamic control

In plain English: When a reaction can make two different products, the one that forms fastest is not always the most stable one. Cold, quick, one-way conditions give the fast (kinetic) product; warm, long, reversible conditions let everything settle into the most stable (thermodynamic) product.

Analogy: Two exits from a stadium: a near exit with a short line (low Ea, kinetic product) and a far exit that leads to a nicer parking lot (more stable, thermodynamic product). If everyone is in a hurry and cannot come back (low T, irreversible), most take the near exit. If people can wander back and forth for hours (high T, reversible), they end up in the nicer lot.

Official definition: Under kinetic control (low temperature, short time, irreversible conditions) the major product is the one formed fastest (lowest Ea); under thermodynamic control (higher temperature, longer time, reversible conditions) the major product is the most stable one (most negative ΔG°).

Core idea (3 points):

  • Two different winners: kinetic product = lower Ea; thermodynamic product = lower G (more stable), even if its barrier is higher.
  • Classic example: HBr + 1,3-butadiene: at −80 °C the 1,2-adduct dominates (kinetic); at 40 °C the 1,4-adduct dominates (thermodynamic, more substituted alkene).
  • Can vs. will: diamond → graphite has ΔG° < 0 but a huge Ea: thermodynamics says "can," kinetics says "not in our lifetime."
Kinetic product ratio ≈ k₁/k₂ = e<sup>(Ea₂ − Ea₁)/RT</sup> (same A)Thermodynamic ratio = e<sup>−(ΔG°₁ − ΔG°₂)/RT</sup>

In plain words: under kinetic control, the product ratio is set by how much lower one barrier is; under thermodynamic control, it is set by how much more stable one product is.

When to use it: "which product dominates at low vs. high temperature?", or "by what factor is product 1 favored given the two Ea values (or two ΔG° values)?". When it does not apply: the kinetic form assumes the same A for both paths and irreversible conditions; the thermodynamic form assumes the products interconvert and have reached equilibrium. Use J/mol with R = 8.314 and T in kelvin.

C) 3 MCAT-STYLE PRACTICE QUESTIONS

Q1. For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it spontaneous?

  • A) 0.4 K
  • B) 40 K
  • C) 400 K
  • D) 4,000 K

Answer: C. ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 40,000 J/mol ÷ 100 J/(mol·K) = 400 K. Above that, TΔS > ΔH.

  • A is wrong: it divides 40 kJ by 100 without converting kJ to J.
  • B is wrong: it converts 40 kJ to 4,000 J instead of 40,000 J.
  • C is correct.
  • D is wrong: it converts 40 kJ to 400,000 J (one extra factor of 10).

Q2. Initial-rate data for A + B → C: doubling [A] at constant [B] quadruples the rate; doubling [B] at constant [A] has no effect. What is the rate law?

  • A) Rate = k[A][B]
  • B) Rate = k[A]²
  • C) Rate = k[A]²[B]
  • D) Rate = k[B]

Answer: B. 2ˣ = 4 → x = 2; 2ʸ = 1 → y = 0.

  • A is wrong: first order in A would only double the rate.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: B is zero order.
  • D is wrong: the rate depends on A, not B.

Q3. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of NH₃ and changes K?

  • A) Raising the temperature
  • B) Lowering the temperature
  • C) Compressing the container
  • D) Adding an iron catalyst

Answer: B. For an exothermic reaction, lowering T favors products and raises K.

  • A is wrong: raising T favors the endothermic (reverse) direction and lowers K.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: compression raises yield (4 gas moles → 2) but does not change K.
  • D is wrong: catalysts speed approach to equilibrium without shifting it or changing K.
